docs.title: SuperPuTTY
docs.text:
SuperPuTTY turns PuTTY into a tabbed, dockable session manager. It starts PuTTY (or KiTTY, Mintty, Cygterm, a VNC viewer) as a normal program and embeds its window as a tab, so dozens of SSH, Telnet or serial sessions can be arranged, saved and restored in one main window.

This is the Kraus-Ahma IT Consulting edition: the original SuperPuTTY, ported to .NET 10, with tools for day-to-day administration of many Linux hosts.

Help for the window you are in

Press F1 in a pane or dialog (Sessions, Host Info, Containers, Run on Hosts …) to open its page.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text: Topic What it covers Sessions Organise sessions in folders, search them, reopen the last ten with one click Tabs and layouts Dock terminals side by side, save arrangements, see prod/qual/dev at a glance Icon bar Every tool as an icon — choose and order them yourself Command bar Send a command to one, several or all terminals; type into all of them at once Commands pane A library of reusable commands with placeholders, per host, folder or for all Run on Hosts Run one command on many hosts in the background and compare the results Host Info Live CPU, memory, disks, GPUs, users and processes of the active tab's host Containers Docker containers of the host: shells, logs, start/stop, open ports in the browser Health Disk, memory, load, failed units and containers checked; notified when a host turns red SSH tunnels Tunnels of every tab with their state File transfer Drag files onto a tab, copy between PC and hosts or from host to host Copy, logs, Claude Copy a session or the last command, keep session logs, ask Claude about output

docs.title: Requirements in short
docs.text:
• Windows 10/11 x64 with the .NET 10 Desktop Runtime.
  • PuTTY or KiTTY. PSCP for file transfer; plink (comes with PuTTY) for everything that runs in the background — Host Info, Containers, health checks, Run on Hosts. These background features need key-based login (e.g. Pageant) and a host key PuTTY has already accepted; see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Command bar
docs.text:
The text field next to the icon bar sends a command to terminals. By default it goes to the active tab; the selector next to it sends to all tabs that accept commands (tab context menu) or to the visible ones.

  • Enter sends the command and Enter, the arrow keys pick earlier commands.
  • The history is kept per session and login (up to 50 entries, saved across restarts; age limit in Options, 0 = no limit).
  • When production tabs are among the targets, SuperPuTTY asks first.

docs.title: Live input
docs.text:
The keyboard button in the command bar switches live input on: what you type into one PuTTY tab is typed into all other tabs that accept commands, key by key (in the style of ClusterSSH). Turning it on needs at least two targets and asks first when production tabs are among them.

Ctrl and Alt combinations that SuperPuTTY uses itself (e.g. Ctrl+Tab, Alt+F4) stay local.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Commands pane: reusable commands, typed or run with a click.
  • Run on Hosts: run a command on many hosts without open tabs and compare the output.

docs.title: Commands pane
docs.text: View → Commands. A library of reusable commands, grouped by category, with a filter box.

docs.title: Using a command
docs.text:
Action Effect Click Types the command into the active terminal (without Enter) Double-click / Enter Types and runs it Shift+Enter Types only Right-click Selects it and opens the menu: Run in New Tab, Run in All Terminals, Run in Terminals of Folder, Add to Favorites, Edit, Delete, Move Up/Down, Import, Export

A named command shows its name and, below it in grey, the command itself. The green ▶ marks the row under the mouse.

docs.title: Where a command applies
docs.text: Each command applies to all sessions, a folder of the session tree or one session. The pane shows the commands for the active tab in sections — This session, its folders, All sessions. Commands of deleted sessions or folders appear under Not assigned and can be reassigned with Edit.

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text:
{{name}} or {{name:default}} in a command are asked for before it is sent, e.g.

docker compose --project-directory {{compose dir:~}} logs -f {{service}}

The values are remembered per session. Placeholders are shown in purple. Docker's own templates such as {{.Names}} are left alone.

docs.title: Favorites, import and export
docs.text: Favorites is always listed first. Import adds commands from another Commands.XML (skipping existing ones), Export writes a section or all commands. The library is stored in Commands.XML in the data folder.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text: View → Containers. The docker containers on the active tab's host, grouped by compose project.

docs.title: The list
docs.text: Each container shows a status dot — green running/healthy, amber starting/restarting/paused, red unhealthy or crashed, grey stopped — its name (without the project prefix), its status and uptime, the image, and the published ports as small chips (9089→8080). Project headers count running containers and problems. The stop icon in the toolbar also shows stopped containers.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text: Action Effect Double-click / Enter Shell inside the container in a new tab (bash, else sh) Click a port chip Opens the port in the browser Right-click Root shell, follow logs, inspect, Open in Browser, start/stop/restart (asks first), copy name F5 / refresh icon Reload

docs.title: Opening ports in the browser
docs.text: A click on a port chip opens http://host:port directly when your PC can reach it. Otherwise — the port is bound to the host's 127.0.0.1, blocked by a firewall, or the host is behind a jump host — SuperPuTTY opens an SSH tunnel and opens the browser on localhost. Tunnels are reused and closed when SuperPuTTY exits. Ports 443 and 8443 open with https.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: The list and the actions run through plink: key-based login and a known host key. Without membership in the docker group, SuperPuTTY tries sudo -n docker; container tabs then use sudo and may ask for the password.

docs.title: File transfer
docs.text: All transfers use PSCP (set its location under Options) and run in the background; progress and result appear in the status bar.

docs.title: Upload by drag and drop
docs.text: Drop files or folders from Explorer onto a terminal tab header (or the upload icon). A dialog confirms the target folder — preset with the shell's current directory when the window title shows it (user@host: ~/dir, as Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora set it). Click the upload icon to pick files instead.

docs.title: Transfer Files
docs.text:
Tools → Transfer Files… (or its icon): source and target are each This PC or a session, preset with the active tab and its current directory.

  • PC → host: upload. Host → PC: download.
  • Host → host: copied through this PC (a temporary folder, deleted afterwards), so the hosts need no keys for each other.

docs.title: File browser and external tools
docs.text: The session menu offers a PSCP-based file browser and, if installed, WinSCP or FileZilla for the session.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. Install the .NET 10 Desktop Runtime (x64) and PuTTY (or KiTTY). The PuTTY installer also brings pscp.exe and plink.exe.
  2. Run SuperPuttySetup.msi. A newer version installs over the old one; settings and sessions are kept.

docs.title: First start
docs.text:
SuperPuTTY asks for:

  • the location of putty.exe (or KiTTY) and pscp.exe,
  • the data folder for sessions, layouts and commands (default Documents\SuperPuTTY).

Both can be changed later under Tools → Options.

docs.title: Get your sessions in
docs.text:
• File → Import Sessions → From PuTTY Settings takes the sessions saved in PuTTY.
  • From File imports a SuperPuTTY sessions XML, From PuTTY CM Export a PuTTY Connection Manager export.
  • Or create them yourself: right-click a folder in the Sessions pane → New Session.

Double-click a session to open it as a tab.

docs.title: Recommended for the background tools
docs.text:
Host Info, Containers, health checks and Run on Hosts log in with plink in the background. Set up once:

  • Key-based login: load your key into Pageant. The status bar shows a green dot with the number of keys when Pageant is running with keys.
  • Accept host keys: connect to each host once with a normal tab, so PuTTY knows its key.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
SuperPutty.exe --help lists the options. Examples:

SuperPutty.exe -layout MyLayout
SuperPutty.exe -session "Prod/web01"
SuperPutty.exe -ssh -P 22 -l admin -load MyPuttyProfile web01.example.com

With single-instance mode on (Options → Advanced), further launches open their session in the running SuperPuTTY.

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text:
Check Warning (orange) Critical (red) Disk usage per filesystem from 80 % from 90 % Memory from 85 % from 95 % Load per CPU from 1 from 2 Failed systemd units any — Unhealthy docker containers — any

Problem hosts are coloured in the session tree; folders take the colour of their worst host. The tooltip of a host lists the problems and the last values.

docs.title: When hosts are checked
docs.text:
• Open tabs: automatically, each host at most every five minutes (View → Health Checks for Open Tabs). Every check is an SSH login and appears in the host's auth log, hence the interval.
  • Any session or folder: right-click → Check Health.
  • Host Info updates the host it shows continuously.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: View → Notify When a Host Turns Critical (on by default): a Windows notification when a host becomes critical, and another when it recovers. Warnings don't notify, a failed check doesn't count as recovery, and a host that stays critical is reported once. Several changes at the same time (e.g. after start-up) come as one notification.

docs.title: Host Info
docs.text: View → Host Info (monitor icon). Live facts about the active tab's host, opened as a tab in front of Session Detail.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• Host name, operating system and kernel.
  • Public and private addresses of the host's own network interfaces (container bridges and loopback left out — no outside service is asked).
  • Uptime.
  • CPU usage with the load average; memory with swap; disks (one bar per filesystem, the fullest first, at most six).
  • GPUs on hosts with NVIDIA GPUs: utilisation, VRAM and temperature per GPU, and the processes holding GPU memory.
  • Logged-in users (who, terminal, from where, since when), the number of processes and the busiest ones with their CPU share (like top, 100 % = one CPU).
  • Failed systemd units and unhealthy containers, if any.

The bars use the colours of the health checks: amber and red mean the same everywhere. A GPU bar turns amber/red with its temperature; VRAM only turns amber when practically full, because inference servers reserve most of it on purpose.

Copy puts everything on the clipboard as text, ready for a ticket or chat.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Values Refreshed CPU, load, memory, processes, GPUs every 5 seconds Disks, logged-in users, failed units, containers every 60 seconds Host name, OS, addresses once per connection

Host Info keeps one SSH connection open to the host instead of logging in for every refresh, and only while the pane is visible: it pauses when Host Info is a background tab or SuperPuTTY is minimised, and continues when you come back. The values also update the host's health colour in the session tree.

If the connection fails, the reason is shown and SuperPuTTY tries again after 30 seconds; Reconnect (F5) tries at once.

docs.title: The icon bar
docs.text: Below the menu: one icon per tool. Pane icons are toggles — pressed while the pane is open, click again to close it. Tool icons are greyed out when the tool can't be used right now (e.g. Copy Last Command without a PuTTY tab).

docs.title: Choose your icons
docs.text:
Right-click the icon bar → Customize Icon Bar… (also View → Toolbars → Customize Icon Bar…).

  • Checked tools are shown, in the order of the list; unchecked ones are hidden.
  • Move Up / Move Down change the order.
  • Add Separator inserts a divider line, Add Space an empty gap after the selected entry (several spaces make a wider gap); uncheck one to drop it.
  • Reset to Default brings back the standard bar.

Available tools: Sessions, Session Detail, Host Info, Layouts, Commands, Containers, Log Viewer, Open Session, Recent Sessions, Copy Session, Copy Last Command, Explain in Claude, Open Session Log, Open Log Folder, Upload Files, Transfer Files, SSH Tunnels, Run on Hosts, Toggle Command Mask (shows the command bar's text as ***, e.g. for a password), PuTTY Configuration, Options, Kiosk Mode — every entry of the Tools menu.

The choice is stored in your settings and survives updates.

docs.title: Other toolbars
docs.text: View → Toolbars switches the icon bar and the command bar on or off. The menu bar and the status bar can be hidden under View as well.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text: Tools → Options → Shortcuts assigns keys to actions (open session, switch tab, copy session, kiosk mode …). F11 toggles kiosk mode, F2 opens the options, F1 opens the help for the current pane.

docs.title: Run on Hosts
docs.text: Run one command on many hosts in the background and compare the results in a table — without opening a tab per host.

docs.title: Start
docs.text:
• Right-click a folder in the Sessions pane → Run Command on Hosts… — all sessions of that folder.
  • Tools → Run on Hosts… — the folder of the active tab (all sessions without a tab).

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
1. Uncheck hosts you want to leave out. Sessions that aren't SSH (Telnet, serial …) are skipped.
  2. Enter the command, e.g. df -h / or docker compose ps; set the timeout per host.
  3. Run. Six hosts run at a time; Stop ends the rest.

If production hosts are among the checked ones, SuperPuTTY lists them and asks first.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Result Meaning ● ok Exit code 0 ● exit N The command failed with exit code N (its error output is shown after --- stderr ---) ● error No result: login failed, host key unknown, host unreachable, or the timeout passed stopped / not run / skipped Stopped by you, unchecked, or not an SSH session

Select a host to see its full output below the table. Only failed hides the successful ones. Copy All and Save… produce a text report with every host's output.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Runs through plink like the other background tools: key-based login (Pageant) and known host keys. Hosts that fail with "Cannot confirm a host key" need one normal connection first.

docs.title: Scripts (SPSL)
docs.text: SPSL is a small script language for sending input to terminals — for a login sequence when a session opens, or from the script editor.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
One command per line; # starts a comment.

Command Effect SENDLINE text Types the text and Enter SENDCHAR text Types the text without Enter SENDKEY key Sends a key, e.g. SENDKEY {ENTER} SLEEP ms Waits the given milliseconds OPENSESSION id Opens a session by its id (folder/name) CLOSESESSION Closes the session

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# switch to the application user and its directory
SENDLINE sudo -iu app
SLEEP 500
SENDLINE cd /srv/app && git status

Set a script for a session in its settings (Edit → SPSL Script); it runs when the session opens.

docs.title: The Sessions pane
docs.text:
View → Sessions (or the tree icon in the icon bar). Sessions are organised in folders; double-click opens a session, right-click offers new sessions and folders, rename, connect all sessions of a folder, health checks and Run Command on Hosts.

  • Search: type into the box at the top and press Enter (the ✕ button clears it).
  • Recent sessions: the clock button in front of the search box lists the last 10 opened sessions, newest first, each once, with its folder on the right. A click opens it; Clear List empties it. The same list is available as an icon on the icon bar. Only sessions of the session list count — quick connections and command tabs don't.
  • Health colours: hosts with problems are shown orange or red, folders in the colour of their worst host — see Health.

docs.title: Session Detail
docs.text: Shows the settings of the session selected in the tree, docked below the Sessions pane. It opens and closes together with the Sessions pane. Edit a session with right-click → Edit.

docs.title: Session icons and environments
docs.text:
Each session can have an icon (Edit → Icon). The icons named prod-…, qual-…, dev-… mark the environment — shape = role (server, web, database, docker, GPU, …), colour = environment (prod red, qual amber, dev green). The environment is also taken from folder names such as Prod, Production, QA, Staging or Dev.

The environment shows on the tabs and makes SuperPuTTY ask before a command goes to production hosts.

docs.title: Stored passwords
docs.text: A password can be stored with a session. It is saved encrypted for your Windows user (it can't be used by other users or on other computers) and passed to PuTTY through a short-lived file, never on the command line. Key-based login with Pageant is still the better choice — and the background tools need it.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Tools → Options (F2):

Tab Contains General Locations of PuTTY/KiTTY, PSCP, Mintty, VNC viewer, WinSCP, FileZilla; PuTTY default parameters; the data folder; default layout GUI Session tree, tabs and docking, session panel, command bar history, file transfer prefixes, Security (Pass stored passwords to PuTTY), tray and other options, Reconnect dropped sessions automatically Shortcuts Keyboard shortcuts for actions Advanced Application behaviour (single instance and more), focus handling

The View menu holds the switches for health checks, notifications, session logs, background activity, toolbars and kiosk mode.

docs.title: Where things are stored
docs.text:
What Where Settings SuperPuTTY.settings in your user folder (%USERPROFILE%) Sessions Sessions.XML in the data folder (default Documents\SuperPuTTY) Layouts layouts\ in the data folder Commands Commands.XML in the data folder Session logs logs\ in the data folder

Portable: put SuperPuTTY.settings next to SuperPutty.exe (and no copy in your user folder) — the installation then keeps its settings with it.

docs.title: Back up and restore
docs.text: File → Back up Settings… writes one zip with the settings, sessions, commands and layouts (no logs). File → Restore Settings… saves the current state to backups\ in the data folder first and applies the backup on the next start. Stored passwords only decrypt for the same Windows user.

docs.title: Pageant indicator
docs.text: The status bar shows whether Pageant is running and how many keys it holds: green dot with the number of keys, amber when it has no keys (or doesn't answer), grey when it isn't running.

docs.title: SSH tunnels
docs.text: Port forwardings of a session — from its PuTTY profile (Connection → SSH → Tunnels) and -L, -R, -D in its extra arguments — are shown on its tab and checked every five seconds.

docs.title: On the tab
docs.text:
Marker Meaning ↔2 Two tunnels, all fine ↔2! A local tunnel isn't listening, or its port is held by another program or a tab of another host

The tab's tooltip lists every tunnel with its state. A port held by another tab of the same host (e.g. a duplicate) counts as fine. Remote tunnels (-R) can't be checked from this PC. The first 20 seconds after opening a tab aren't reported (PuTTY opens the ports after login).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Tools → SSH Tunnels… lists the tunnels of all open tabs; Go to Tab jumps to the tab.

docs.title: Temporary tunnels for containers
docs.text: Opening a container port that isn't reachable directly creates its own tunnel — see Containers.

docs.title: Arranging terminals
docs.text: Every session opens as a tab. Drag a tab to dock it beside or below others, or out of the window to float it. Tool panes (Sessions, Commands, Host Info …) dock the same way.

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text: A layout saves the arrangement of open sessions and panes. File → Save Layout / Save Layout As, the Layouts pane lists them. A layout can be restored on start-up (Options) or from the command line (-layout Name).

docs.title: Tab markers
docs.text: Marker Meaning Coloured bar Environment: prod red (with a red !), qual amber, dev green ↔2 The session opens 2 SSH tunnels; ↔2! = one of them isn't working — see SSH tunnels ● Something changed in a background tab (title changed, e.g. a command finished) × The connection dropped

docs.title: Environment markers
docs.text: Production tabs get a red bar and badge, and commands sent to several terminals ask for confirmation when production hosts are among them.

docs.title: Background activity
docs.text:
View → Mark Background Tab Activity (on by default). When SuperPuTTY isn't the active window, a Windows notification appears as well. Most shells only change the title at the prompt; to see when a long command finishes, let bash show the running command in the title (~/.bashrc on the server):

trap 'printf "\033]0;%s: %s\007" "${HOSTNAME%%.*}" "$BASH_COMMAND"' DEBUG

docs.title: Reconnect
docs.text: When a connection drops, the tab is marked × and a yellow bar offers Reconnect. With Options → GUI → Reconnect dropped sessions automatically SuperPuTTY retries after 5, 10, 20, 40 and 60 seconds (up to six times). Key and Pageant logins reconnect silently; password sessions ask again.

docs.title: Kiosk mode
docs.text: F11 (or the kiosk icon) shows only the terminal tabs, full screen. F11 again restores everything.

docs.title: Copy, logs and Explain in Claude
Copy a session
docs.text: Tools → Copy Session to Clipboard (or its icon) copies the active terminal's screen and scrollback as plain text — commands and output, e.g. for a ticket. Only what is still in PuTTY's scrollback is copied (2000 lines by default, set in the PuTTY profile).

docs.title: Copy the last command
docs.text: Tools → Copy Last Command copies only the last command and its output. SuperPuTTY recognises usual prompts (user@host:dir$, [user@host dir]#, user@host dir %, with an optional (venv) in front); without a recognised prompt the whole session is copied.

docs.title: Session logs
docs.text:
View → Log Sessions to Files writes every new tab's output to a file in the logs folder of the data folder. The raw .log contains terminal control codes; when the tab closes, a readable .txt is written next to it. Tools → Open Session Log opens the active tab's log as text, Open Log Folder the folder.

Note

Typed passwords aren't echoed by the server and therefore not logged — but everything the terminal displayed is.

docs.title: Explain in Claude
docs.text:
Tools → Explain in Claude… takes the last command and its output and shows it in an editable window — nothing is sent until you press Send. Remove anything confidential first. Claude's explanation streams into the window, in the language of your question.

Needs an Anthropic API key: API Key… in that window stores it encrypted for your Windows user; otherwise the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable is used.

docs.title: Background tools fail (Host Info, Containers, health, Run on Hosts)
docs.text:
These tools log in with plink in batch mode: they never ask, they fail.

Message Cause and fix plink.exe was not found Install PuTTY with its tools; plink must be next to putty.exe or on the PATH The host key is not known yet / Cannot confirm a host key in batch mode Open the session once as a normal tab and accept the host key Background login failed / Access denied Use key-based login: load the key into Pageant (status bar shows the key count) or set -i keyfile in the session's extra arguments No access to docker on this host Add the user to the docker group, or allow sudo docker without a password bash: <host>: command not found Fixed since 1.5.1: happened with sessions whose PuTTY profile stores the host name

Passwords are only passed to plink when Options → GUI → Security → Pass stored passwords to PuTTY is on — keys are the better way.

docs.title: A tab stays empty or PuTTY opens outside
docs.text: SuperPuTTY embeds the program's window after it appears. Programs that open their window very late or start a second process (e.g. newer Mintty) may not be caught. Check the executable paths under Options.

docs.title: Drag and drop onto the terminal does nothing
docs.text: PuTTY's window belongs to another program, so Windows may not pass drops on it to SuperPuTTY. Drop onto the tab header or the upload icon instead.

docs.title: Log files
docs.text: SuperPuTTY writes a log to %TEMP%\SuperPuTTY.<date_time>.log. View → Log Viewer shows it live inside SuperPuTTY; Help → Diagnostics shows version and environment details. Attach both to a bug report.
